messages.subject: Using add_generator from_to convenience function with own distribution fit
parts:
Hi there,

Quite new to simmer, but the package and community both look great! 

I have been having some trouble implementing my own pseudo 'distribution' function in the dist function() requirement of the add_generator's from_to convenience function.

Here is my current generator setup:

processingcentre.env <- simmer() %>%
  add_resource("staff", numstaff[1], queue_size=Inf, capacity= capacity_schedule, preempt_order = c("fifo")) %>%
  add_generator("Monday", customer.trajectory,from_to2(0,24,function() distribution_fit('mon',Mondata,dailylambda[1],0),arrive=FALSE, every=168)) %>%   #swap Mondata with sample(0:24,7)
  add_generator("Tuesday", customer.trajectory,from_to2(24,48, function() distribution_fit('tue',Tuedata,dailylambda[2],0),arrive=FALSE, every=168)) %>%   # swap Tuedata sample(24:48,7)
  add_generator("Wednesday", customer.trajectory,from_to2(48,72, function() distribution_fit('wed',Weddata,dailylambda[3],0),arrive=FALSE, every=168)) %>%  #..           sample(48:72,7)
  add_generator("Thursday", customer.trajectory,from_to2(72,96,function() distribution_fit('thu',Thudata,dailylambda[4],0),arrive=FALSE, every=168)) %>%     #            sample(72:96,7)
  add_generator("Friday", customer.trajectory,from_to2(96,120, function() distribution_fit('fri',Fridata,dailylambda[5],0),arrive=FALSE, every=168)) %>%      #           sample(96:120,7)
  add_generator("Saturday", customer.trajectory,from_to2(120,144, function() distribution_fit('sat',Satdata,dailylambda[6],0),arrive=FALSE, every=168)) %>%   #           sample(120:144,7)
  add_generator("Sunday", customer.trajectory,from_to2(144,168, function() distribution_fit('sun',Sundata,dailylambda[7],0),arrive=FALSE, every=168))         #           sample(144:168,7)
 
run(processingcentre.env,until= runtime)


As you will see, distribution_fit is the controlling interarrival time function

As I have a constantly updating client arrival time database that will be continually built on, I did not think it was wise to choose a distribution (eg. beta, exp, poisson) as this distribution will change over time as I get more data (and very likely seasonally change).

I opted to attempt to build a distribution function which would take all data, take a sample() from the data, and then spit out INTER arrival times.

Here is that function:

distribution_fit <- function(dayofweek,dayofweekarrivaldata,dailylamamount,dailydeviation){
  startdayminus <- data.frame(0,25,49,73,97,121,145,168)
  if (dayofweek == 'mon') { startdayminus <- as.numeric(startdayminus[1])
  } else if (dayofweek == 'tue') { startdayminus <- as.numeric(startdayminus[2]) #subtract start of day
  } else if (dayofweek == 'wed') { startdayminus <- as.numeric(startdayminus[3])
  } else if (dayofweek == 'thu') { startdayminus <- as.numeric(startdayminus[4])
  } else if (dayofweek == 'fri') { startdayminus <- as.numeric(startdayminus[5])
  } else if (dayofweek == 'sat') { startdayminus <- as.numeric(startdayminus[6])
  } else if (dayofweek == 'sun') { startdayminus <- as.numeric(startdayminus[7])}
  
  if (count == 0) {
    
    a <<- as.data.frame(table(dayofweekarrivaldata[,3]))    #get hour of day a[1], and frequency of occurence as count [a2]
    dayhour <<- as.numeric(as.character(a$Var1))     #get hour of day
    freqper <<- as.vector(t(t(a[[2]]) / sum(a[[2]]))) #turn frequency of occurrence into percent
    answer1 <<- sort(sample(dayhour, size = rnorm(1,mean= dailylamamount,sd=dailydeviation), replace = TRUE, prob = freqper)) #get a sample from known arrivals
    answer2 <<- as.vector(c(startdayminus,answer1))
    answer <<- diff(answer2)
    answer[answer == 0] <<- 0.01
    
    if (sum(answer) >= 23) { answer <<- ifelse(answer != 0.01,answer-(0.01*length(answer)),answer)}
    
    count <<- count+1
    
    return(answer[count])
    
  } else {
    
    count <<- count+1
    
    if (count <= length(answer)) {
      return(answer[count])
    } else  { 
      count <<- 0
      return(-1)   #is this right to stop the generator?
    }
  }
} 


As you can see, the function produces an answer, and if there are 0's (same arrival time of customer) adds a little 0.01 (as im not sure what effect a 0 has on inter-arrival time. Once count reaches above the length of answer (which == desired daily number of customers), it returns a -1 which as far as I know should stop the generator. This should then reset the count, and move on to the next generator.

When I run a single day, so just monday, I see the expected results. I get the number of applications I should receive at the times I can see have been formulated in my function. However, when i string days together it goes haywire. Results are not as expected and unexplainable arrivals are occuring, and it does not stick to the daily number of arrivals.

I cannot figure out for the life of me why.. I am not quite understanding how the from_to is retrieving from the internal function.

Any help would be appreciated in how to implement this correctly. Let me know if this is reproducible and a clear explanation.

Also, any comments, queries or suggestions based on how I could do this would be appreciated. I am wanting to run many weeks to months of simulation.

Forward thanks for any interactions, and again thank you for a brilliant simulation package!


Kindest regards
Joe

joseph...@adelaide.edu.au

It's ok to return zeroes. A bunch of zeroes will produce a bunch of
arrivals at the same time, just as expected.

> has on inter-arrival time. Once count reaches above the length of answer

> as I know should stop the generator. This should then reset the count, and

First of all, yes: returning -1 stops the generator. But as far as I
understand, you don't want to stop the generators, but just to spit
arrivals at certain periods. Moreover, if you use one of these
convenience functions, you should *never* return -1, because the
convenience function will do it for you if it's required (functions
"at" and "to", and also "from_to" if there's no period defined, i.e.,
every=NULL).

In this case, there's a period defined (the week), so from_to won't
return -1 and your distribution shouldn't either. from_to works by
accumulating the interarrival times returned by the distribution
function you provide, and only produces arrivals in the periods
defined. For example, check this code:

generator <- from_to(0, 2, function() rexp(100, 1), arrive=FALSE, every=10)
interarrivals <- unlist(replicate(10, generator()))
plot(cumsum(interarrivals), seq_along(interarrivals))

As you can see in the graph, the distribution provided just returns
interarrivals, exponentially distributed in this case, but does not
know a thing about the period. And yet, from_to manages to spit these
interarrivals between (0, 2), (10, 12), (20, 22), etc.

Therefore, in your case, you just need to sample from your data. Something like

from_to(0, 24, function() sample(monday_data, ...), arrive=FALSE, every=168)
from_to(24, 48, function() sample(tuesday_data, ...), arrive=FALSE, every=168)
...

and so on and so forth. This sampling function may return a single
interarrival per call or a bunch of them: it doesn't matter, because
"from_to" will cut and insert a leap in the right place. In fact, it's
better to return many interarrival times per call for the sake of
performance.

This was the from_to() function I found you posted somewhere else:


from_to2 <- function(start_time, stop_time, dist, arrive=TRUE, every=NULL) {
  stopifnot(is.null(every) || every >= stop_time)
  started <- FALSE
  init <- 0
  counter <- 0
  function() {
    while (TRUE){
      if (!started) {
        started <<- TRUE
        if (arrive) {
          dt <- start_time - init
        } else {
          dt <- dist()
          dt[1] <- dt[1] + start_time - init
        }
      } else {
        dt <- dist()
      }
      len <- length(dt)
      dt <- dt[cumsum(dt) + counter < stop_time]
      counter <<- counter + sum(dt)
      if (len == length(dt))
        return(dt)
      if (is.null(every))
        return(c(dt, -1))
      if (length(dt))
        return(dt)
      start_time <<- start_time + every
      stop_time <<- stop_time + every
      started <<- FALSE
      init <<- counter
    }
  }
}

general. Because what you get from that is not the original arrival
process, but a kind of decimation of the original.

> I then add on to this the first hour of
> the day, so for mondays this is 0, tuesdays this is 24, wednesdays is 48 etc

You don't need to do that, because you are going to take differences.
Just add a zero at the beginning, always.

> Then my monday_data is calculated as diff(0,6,9,12,12,14,15,18) to give me
> an interarrival list time of 6,3,3,3,1,1,3.

I suppose you meant 6, 3, 3, 0, 2, 1, 3. As I said, it is ok to return
a zero, you don't need to add 0.01 or something like that.

> When I am passing the sample data straight in as a singular group of
> numbers, from what I can see it is taking the interarrival list and using
> the lowest interarrivals first and progressing to higher interarrival times.
> Is this how it works? maybe I am confused??
> So the customer ends up arriving at 1am(1), 2am (1), 5am(3) ,8am(3) etc etc,
> instead of using the sorted list order.

No, it's not. from_to takes the interarrivals and uses them in the
given order. Try it out yourself:

gen <- from_to(0, 24, function() c(6, 3, 3, 0, 2, 1, 3), arrive=FALSE,
every=168)
gen() # first week
#> [1] 6 3 3 0 2 1 3
gen() # second week
#> [1] 156 3 3 0 2 1 3

etc. As you can see, from_to returns exactly the interarrivals given.
It's just adding the appropriate lag between weeks.

return the diffs. That's all. The rest is handled by from_to.

Thank you Iñaki,

I have been continuing to refine and have taken on your advice, however I am still having trouble with the following:

Your example:

gen <- from_to(0, 24, function() c(6, 3, 3, 0, 2, 1, 3), arrive=FALSE, 
every=168) 
gen() # first week 
#> [1] 6 3 3 0 2 1 3 
gen() # second week 
#> [1] 156   3   3   0   2   1   3
gen() # third week
#> [1] 156   3   3   0   2   1   3

etc.etc 

 
I can recreate this and understand how it works taking the sum of the first week, subtracting it from the 'every' value and that starting the next week: however if I apply a function alike to my own I am not getting the same results:
 
gen <- from_to(0, 24, function() rexp(4,rate=1), arrive=FALSE, 
every=168) 
> gen()
[1] 1.7892184 1.0443472 3.3731202 0.6300846
> gen()
[1] 0.7040445 2.7475520 1.0141126 1.5982314


Can I not use from_to to apply dynamic functions to?

When I run this function, it also does not just use the 4 values for the 0 to 24 and move on to the next week ,it continues to call the rexp values and produce as many arrivals as it can within the time window.

Many thanks again and kindest regards
Joe

Note that, in this case, 6 + 3 + 3 + 0 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 6 > 24, and
that's why the second call changes to the next week.

>

> however if I apply a function alike to my own I am not getting the same

>> gen()
> [1] 0.7040445 2.7475520 1.0141126 1.5982314
>
>

> Can I not use from_to to apply dynamic functions to?
You can.

> When I run this function, it also does not just use the 4 values for the 0
> to 24 and move on to the next week ,it continues to call the rexp values and
> produce as many arrivals as it can within the time window.

Exactly. That's how it works. If you need another behaviour, you'll
have to implement your own from_to function.
